episodes.title: INP Final — The forecast
episodes.blurb: There is no case booklet and no posted short-answer question, so this episode is a forecast. Every track is a question the lecturers pointed at: their Exam Content themes, the two revision decks (Lisa’s and Janine’s), the 27 Oct revision session, and their own Canvas quizzes. Each short answer is built the way Lisa taught on 27 Oct: find the command word, use the question’s keywords, about 150 words. Every track says why it is in.
episodes.when: The final: Mon 2 Nov · 40 multi-choice + 15 short answers (about 4 marks each) · 2 h 30 · 50%

chapters.title: How this forecast works
chapters.why: The lecturers have published no short-answer questions for INP. This track explains how the rest were chosen: the Exam Content page, both revision decks, the 27 Oct session and the lecturers' own quizzes.

chapters.title: Social determinants of health
chapters.why: Top of Lisa's list on 27 Oct, the first topic the class voted for, and three lines of the Exam Content page (social and economic determinants, inequalities and inequities, inequalities in Aotearoa). The lecturers' quiz on it is the biggest block in their bank, 14 questions.

show.ask: Define the social determinants of health. Identify two determinants and explain how each one affects health.

t: Definition: the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live and age; the wider forces and systems shaping daily life
Income and the social gradient: lower socioeconomic position, worse health and shorter life expectancy
Work and unemployment: less financial security; poor, unsafe conditions
Stress: chronic fight or flight harms the heart, immunity and mental health
Education: better jobs, income and health literacy
Early life: childhood trauma leads to mental illness and obesity, then CVD and type 2 diabetes
Social exclusion: discrimination limits work, leads to homelessness and the poverty cycle
Health system, transport, conflict, food security, addiction

chapters.title: Equity, equality, inequality, inequity
chapters.why: Lisa's deck gives these four words a slide each and she quizzed them on 27 Oct. Health inequalities and inequities is an Exam Content theme, and equity runs through the Health Strategy, Te Tiriti and screening tracks too.

show.ask: Compare health equality and health equity, and explain the difference between a health inequality and a health inequity, using an example from Aotearoa New Zealand.

t: Equality: everyone gets the same
Equity: fairness; resources go out by need, to close the gap (the different-sized boxes)
Inequality: a difference in health between groups
Inequity: a difference that is unfair and avoidable, from social conditions, and could be reduced by the right policies
Example: Māori and Pacific adults twice as likely not to collect a prescription because of cost; higher diabetes complication rates

chapters.title: Levels of prevention, upstream to downstream
chapters.why: "Theory of Health Promotion, upstream, midstream, downstream factors" is an Exam Content theme that no lecturer quiz asks. Lisa joined it to the levels of prevention on 27 Oct and quizzed it, and her deck spends five slides on it.

show.ask: Describe the four levels of prevention, link each to upstream, midstream or downstream, and give a nursing example of each.

t: Primordial: stops risk factors developing; the social determinants; upstream; advocating for warm, dry housing (Healthy Homes)
Primary: prevents disease where risk exists; populations and high-risk groups; upstream to midstream; vaccination, health education, PPE
Secondary: screening, early detection to stop progression; midstream; cervical screening, mammograms
Tertiary: manage existing disease, prevent it getting worse; downstream; supporting diabetes management
Work at every level at once

chapters.title: Population health, demography and epidemiology
chapters.why: Personal health versus population health, and demography and epidemiology, are two Exam Content themes, both voted for by the class and quizzed by Lisa on 27 Oct. Her slides give the definitions, the two study types and epidemic versus endemic.

show.ask: Differentiate between population health and personal health, and explain how demography and epidemiology help nurses plan care for a population.

t: Population health: health outcomes of a group and how they are distributed; actions for the whole population
Personal health: one individual's risk factors and circumstances; one-to-one care
Public health: the approaches used to improve a population's health (Te Pou Hauora Tūmatanui)
Demography: size, distribution and structure (fertility, mortality, migration, marriage, social mobility)
Epidemiology: patterns, causes and control of disease in groups; observational or experimental
Ageing population: more aged care, multimorbidity, workforce planning
Epidemic: more cases than expected; endemic: stable, expected level

chapters.title: Health screening
chapters.why: An Exam Content theme, taught on 20 Oct and quizzed again by Lisa on 27 Oct. Her one sample multi-choice in the revision deck is about screening: what a false negative means.

show.ask: Explain the purpose of health screening, give one organised and one opportunistic example, and discuss why some people do not take part and what nurses can do about it.

t: Purpose: find people at risk or with disease before symptoms; reduces the chance of developing or dying from it
Organised (National Screening Unit): antenatal, newborn metabolic (heel prick), newborn hearing, cervical, breast (45 to 69, two-yearly), bowel
Opportunistic: STI checks, prostate checks, blood pressure
False negative: has the condition but is told they don't; more dangerous than a false positive
Barriers: cost, distance and transport, not knowing what happens, resources only in English
Equity: mobile clinics, self-testing (home bowel kits, cervical self-swabs); nurse educates, assesses and supports

chapters.title: Primary health care and health promotion
chapters.why: "Principles of Primary Health Care" and "Theory of Health Promotion" are both Exam Content themes. Lisa taught the five principles and the health promotion continuum and quizzed them on 27 Oct. No lecturer quiz in the bank asks either, so the short answer is the likely place.

show.ask: Identify the five principles of primary health care and describe how a nurse could apply each one in a community setting.

t: Accessibility: physical access, cost, transport, digital access, appointment times
Community participation: meet the community, find its needs, let people shape services (whānau shaping health plans)
Health promotion: education, nutrition, pamphlets, conversations, campaigns
Appropriate technology: telehealth, online consults
Intersectoral collaboration: working beyond health, with housing, education, transport, government
Continuum: health education, screening, community action, social marketing, influencing policy

chapters.title: The 2023 Health Strategy
chapters.why: "2023 Health Strategy" is an Exam Content theme and was on Lisa's revision list. The deck's own learning outcomes say identify and describe the two goals and the six priorities, which is exactly how a short answer would be worded. The lecturers' Practice Quizzes ask the Act it sits under.

show.ask: Identify the two long-term goals of the New Zealand Health Strategy 2023 and describe how one of its priority areas applies to nursing practice.

t: Vision: pae ora, healthy futures; under the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022
Goal 1: achieve health equity, especially for Māori, Pacific, disabled people and others with poorer outcomes
Goal 2: improve health outcomes for all, so everyone lives longer, healthier, more independent lives
Six priorities: voice at the heart of the system; flexible, appropriate care; valuing our workforce; a learning culture; a resilient and sustainable system; partnerships for health and wellbeing
Example: voice at the heart, so the person and whānau shape the plan

chapters.title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and cultural safety
chapters.why: Lisa ended her 27 Oct list on the articles of Te Tiriti and gave them two slides. "Cultural awareness and sensitivity" sits on the Exam Content page beside therapeutic use of self, and the Population Health deck says outright never to use the three Ps.

show.ask: Identify the three articles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi and explain how one of the five principles guides a nurse's practice with Māori patients and whānau.

t: Article 1, kāwanatanga: governance; Māori in decision-making
Article 2, tino rangatiratanga: Māori autonomy; control over knowledge, language and customs as taonga
Article 3, ōritetanga: equity for Māori
Five principles (Waitangi Tribunal 2019): tino rangatiratanga, mana taurite (equity), whakamarumarutia (active protection), kōwhiringa (options), pātuitanga (partnership)
The three Ps (1986) are outdated
Cultural safety, kawa whakaruruhau: the patient decides whether care is safe

chapters.title: Standards of competence, scope and roles of nurses
chapters.why: "Standards of Competence and BN2 student nurse scope of practice", "Roles of nurses", "Nursing informatics" and "Continuum of care" are four Exam Content themes. Lisa listed competencies and roles on 27 Oct, and the lecturers' Practice Quizzes ask scope twice: both answers are decline.

show.ask: Identify the six pou of the Registered Nurse Standards of Competence and explain the scope of practice of a BN2 student nurse, with an example.

t: Six pou: Māori health; cultural safety (kawa whakaruruhau); whanaungatanga and communication; pūkengatanga and evidence-informed practice; manaakitanga and people-centred care; rangatiratanga and leadership
Each pou has descriptors, examples of evidence of competence
Student scope: work under an RN's direction and supervision, only what you've been taught and assessed as competent in
Decline a doctor's telephone order; decline a preceptor's request to give an overdue paracetamol
Roles: aged care, primary and community, acute, mental health, informatics; continuum of care

chapters.title: Therapeutic use of self and emotional intelligence
chapters.why: Lisa's worked practice question on 27 Oct was emotional intelligence and therapeutic communication, with a model answer on her slide. She said it was made up and not in the exam, but therapeutic use of self is an Exam Content theme and was on her revision list, so the same topic in other words is likely.

show.ask: Explain the role of emotional intelligence and discuss its impact on therapeutic communication in nursing practice.

t: EI: recognising, understanding and managing your own emotions while responding appropriately to others
Hierarchy: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills
Therapeutic use of self: personal insight, presence and authenticity to build trust; acknowledge your own bias
Rests on competent communication and emotional intelligence
Impact: empathy and trust, better understanding of needs, patient-centred care, manages challenging interactions, less conflict, better outcomes

chapters.title: Family-centred care
chapters.why: "Family centered care" is an Exam Content theme and was on Lisa's 27 Oct list. Her deck gives a definition and three principles; the lecturers' Practice Quiz asks a principle (partnership).

show.ask: Define family in the context of family-centred care and describe the three principles that make up a partnership with the person and their family.

t: Family: whoever the person identifies as family, with or without biological or legal ties; blended, single-parent, shared care, same-sex, extended
Relationship: genuine and mutually respectful
Participation and involvement: respect the autonomy of the person and family
Tailoring care: to their needs, strengths, limits and context
Core: empowerment and advocacy, a Te Tiriti obligation

chapters.title: Pain assessment
chapters.why: "Pain assessment" is named in the Exam Content assessment line, the class voted for it, and it was the first topic on Lisa's slides that she ran out of time to talk through on 27 Oct. The lecturers' Practice Quizzes ask the first thing to do for pain: assess it with a scale.

show.ask: Describe the difference between acute and chronic pain and explain how a nurse would assess a patient's pain.

t: Pain: an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked to actual or potential tissue damage; what the person says it is
Acute: rapid onset, under 6 months, resolves as it heals
Chronic: over 6 months, non-life-threatening cause, sometimes unknown; can lead to depression and anxiety
Nociceptive (somatic: localised, sharp; visceral: diffuse, crampy) vs neuropathic (shooting, burning)
OLDCARTS: onset, location, duration, characteristics, aggravating, relieving, treatment, severity
Scales: 0 to 10 numerical, at rest and on movement; Wong-Baker faces for children, non-verbal or language barrier
Assess every time you check on the patient

chapters.title: Discharge planning
chapters.why: "Discharge planning" is an Exam Content theme, the class voted for it, and it is on Lisa's slides. No lecturer question exists, and the lecture's Cyril Lear scenario is the closest thing in the course to a ready-made short answer.

show.ask: Explain why discharge planning starts on admission and describe what a nurse would include in a patient's discharge plan.

t: Starts at admission: an interdisciplinary process for continuity of care and a smooth transition
Reduces readmissions, length of stay and community follow-up needed
Nurse coordinates; often the last point of contact
Process: assess, plan and prepare, implement, evaluate

Include: mode of discharge, self-care (medicines, diet, wounds, pain), equipment settings, follow-up appointments, permitted activities (lifting, driving), warning signs and what to do, health promotion
Patient and family understand and agree

chapters.title: The nursing process and care planning
chapters.why: "Nursing process: Nursing care planning" is an Exam Content theme and opens Janine's revision deck (slides 3 to 10). Learning outcome 1 is apply the nursing process, and it returns in holistic assessment and discharge planning. The quiz only asks you to recognise a good diagnosis or goal; writing one is the short-answer risk.

show.ask: Describe the five steps of the nursing process and compare a medical diagnosis with a nursing diagnosis.

t: ADPIE: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation
Assessment: observation, interview, examination; objective (signs) and subjective (symptoms); primary, secondary, tertiary sources
Diagnosis: actual or potential problems nursing can prevent, reduce or resolve; NANDA-I; prioritised
Planning: SMART short- and long-term goals; restate the diagnosis as improvement
Implementation: evidence-based, safe, within scope, compatible with medical orders
Evaluation: goal met, partly met, not met; timed, dated, signed; ongoing
Medical diagnosis names the disease; nursing diagnosis names the response the nurse can manage (Risk for infection)

chapters.title: Holistic assessment, falls and wounds
chapters.why: The Exam Content line "emergency, holistic, pain, wound and fall risk assessment" names five assessments. Lisa's one marked practice question on 27 Oct was falls prevention, with her marking guide on slide 101. Janine's deck gives the Morse Fall Scale and the wound TIME mnemonic, which no lecturer quiz asks.

show.ask: An older patient has become unsteady when mobilising to the bathroom. Identify and describe five nursing strategies used to prevent falls, and explain how they reduce harm and improve patient outcomes.

t: Lisa's marking guide: 1 mark identify five, 1 mark describe five, 2 marks explain
Assess falls risk (Morse Fall Scale)
Keep the environment free of hazards: clear path to the bathroom
Call bell within reach, and teach how and when to use it
Appropriate mobility aids: physio referral
Assist with mobilising; non-slip socks
Reduce injury, maintain independence, improve safety, prevent fractures, longer stays and loss of confidence
Morse: history of falling, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, IV or heparin lock, gait, mental status; 0 none, under 25 low, 25 to 45 moderate, over 45 high
Wound TIME: tissue, inflammation or infection, moisture, edges

chapters.title: Informed consent
chapters.why: "Informed consent" is an Exam Content theme with nine slides in Janine's revision deck (21 to 28). The lecturers' quiz asks it as short scenarios: an interpreter, a change of mind, a patient with dementia, and the age of 16.

show.ask: Define informed consent and discuss the nurse's role in the consent process, including who can give consent.

t: Definition: telling the patient the benefits, risks and alternatives so they can decide; every procedure; written or verbal
Code of Rights Right 7; NZ Bill of Rights Act s11, right to refuse
16 and over consent for themselves; guardian or enduring power of attorney if incompetent; parent or guardian under 16; court order
Mental Health Act 1992: can't consent but has the right to be informed and to an interpreter
Nurse as advocate: interpreter, whānau support, call the team back if information is missing, check understanding and questions; may witness the signature
Can withdraw at any time: stop and notify

chapters.title: Health literacy and patient education
chapters.why: "Health Literacy" and "Patient education" are two Exam Content themes and twelve slides of Janine's revision deck. Half the lecturers' quiz is scenarios with the same answer in different clothes: plain language, show me, teach-back.

show.ask: Define health literacy and describe strategies a nurse can use to educate a patient with low health literacy, including the teach-back method.

t: Personal health literacy: the ability to find, understand and use information and services for health decisions
Organisational: how equitably an organisation enables that
Not determined by intelligence or income
Poor health literacy: less screening, poorer LTC management, more admissions and ED visits
Ask, Build, Check (teach-back, the gold standard): "tell and show me what you understand"
Interpreter, multilingual resources, plain language, 3 to 5 key points, be specific, demonstrate and draw, be positive

chapters.title: Vital signs, the primary survey, glucose and injections
chapters.why: "Vital signs, injections, blood glucose monitoring" and "emergency assessment" are on the Exam Content page, with sixteen slides in Janine's revision deck. The lecturers' quiz asks terms and ranges; injections are named on the themes list but taught only on the Clinical Learning Suite page.

show.ask: Describe the primary survey (A to E) and give the normal adult range for each vital sign it includes.

t: Airway: talking, coughing, blocked, drooling
Breathing: RR 12 to 20, depth, sounds, work of breathing; SpO2 95 to 100%
Circulation: BP systolic 110 to 140, diastolic 60 to 90; pulse 60 to 100, rate, rhythm, strength, equality
Disability: AVPU; GCS 3 to 15 (eye, verbal, motor)
Exposure: temperature 36.5 to 37.5 °C
Blood glucose 4 to 7.5 mmol/L; hypo under 4
Injections: IM 90°, subcut 45° (90° if 5 cm can be grasped), intradermal 15°; ventrogluteal max 4 mL, deltoid 2 mL or less, vastus lateralis 5 mL

chapters.title: Documentation and ISBAR
chapters.why: "Documentation, Communication (ISBAR(R)/SOAPIER)" is an Exam Content theme with eleven slides in Janine's revision deck. The lecturers' quiz asks rule recall and one applied ISBAR item.

show.ask: Explain why clinical documentation is a legal and professional requirement and describe the ISBAR framework for handing over a deteriorating patient.

t: Legal: HPCA Act 2003, the Code (HDC Act 1994, Right 1 privacy), Privacy Act 2020
Professional: Code of Conduct, pou 3 (legible, accurate, timely)
Not documented = not done; the organisation owns the notes
Label on every page, 24-hour time, sign and designation, blue or black ink, no gaps, one line through errors, no white-out
ISBAR(R): identify, situation, background, assessment, recommendation, review
SOAPIER: subjective, objective, assessment, plan, intervention, evaluation, revision

chapters.title: Infection prevention and control
chapters.why: "Infection prevention and control" is an Exam Content theme and nine slides of Janine's revision deck. The lecturers' quiz asks match-the-precaution vignettes, hand hygiene as the most effective method, and the donning order.

show.ask: Describe the chain of infection and explain how standard and transmission-based precautions break it, with an example of each type of transmission-based precaution.

t: Chain: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host
Standard precautions: minimum for every patient, because you can't tell who is infectious; hand hygiene (most effective), PPE, cough etiquette, sharps, linen and waste, aseptic technique, cleaning
Contact: gown and gloves; MRSA, ESBL, gastro
Droplet: medical mask, eye protection, gown, gloves; influenza, mumps, meningitis
Airborne: N95 respirator, negative-pressure room; measles, chickenpox, TB, COVID-19
HAIs: the most frequently reported adverse event

chapters.title: Evidence-based practice
chapters.why: "Evidence-based practice" is an Exam Content theme, seven slides of Janine's deck, and learning outcome 3 opens with discuss evidence-based practice. The lecturers' quiz asks its goal, its first step and the top of the evidence pyramid.

show.ask: Define evidence-based practice and discuss why it is a professional requirement for nurses, including the levels of evidence.

t: EBP: best research, clinical expertise and patient values, to improve patient outcomes
A shift from opinion and past practice to research and evidence
Pou 4, pūkengatanga and evidence-informed practice; Code of Conduct principle 4 (keep knowledge up to date, reflect)
First step: formulate a clinical question
Levels: expert opinion, qualitative, quantitative, non-randomised trials, RCTs, systematic reviews (strongest)
Databases: CINAHL, Cochrane, JBI, PubMed

chapters.title: Self-care, burnout and compassion fatigue
chapters.why: "Self-care in nursing" is an Exam Content theme and nine slides of Janine's revision deck. The lecturers' quiz can be passed on general knowledge, but the burnout versus compassion fatigue distinction needs the deck, and compare is one of Lisa's command words.

show.ask: Compare burnout and compassion fatigue and describe self-care strategies that build a nurse's resilience.

t: Burnout: an occupational phenomenon from long-term unmanaged workplace stress; exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, reduced professional efficacy; still feel compassion; builds over time
Compassion fatigue: from caring for people who suffer, absorbing their trauma as secondary trauma; loss of empathy; can follow one event; can affect life outside work
Self-care: deliberate, enjoyable, not selfish, needs boundaries
Strategies: realistic goals, let go of some control, change negative thinking, communicate, humour, exercise, 7 to 9 hours' sleep
Resilience: adapting positively to stress; protects against both

chapters.title: Long-term conditions and self-management
chapters.why: "Long term conditions and self-management" is an Exam Content theme and eleven slides of Janine's deck. The lecturers' Long-Term Health Conditions quiz (captured 27 Oct) asks what self-management support must do and the nurse's role: empowering.

show.ask: Define self-management of a long-term condition and describe the nurse's role in self-management support.

t: LTCs: ongoing or recurring; diabetes, cancer, CVD, respiratory, mental illness, chronic pain, CKD, dementia; multimorbidity
Self-management: how a person manages their condition themselves; ongoing; they spend only a few hours a year with services
Support: help to manage day to day, a collaborative partnership
Nurse: information for informed decisions and goals; acknowledge they are experts in their own lives; groups (attend, advocate for); culturally appropriate; follow up; refer
Programmes: health literacy, cultural relevance, behaviour change, the health professional's role

chapters.title: Diabetes and rheumatic fever
chapters.why: "Diabetes, Rheumatic fever" is one line of the Exam Content page, and both close Janine's revision deck. Diabetes is the only disease-specific lecture with a lecturer quiz; rheumatic fever ties straight back to the social determinants.

show.ask: Describe the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes and explain how rheumatic fever develops, who it affects and why.

t: Diabetes: the body can't control blood sugar; not enough insulin, or cells resistant to it
Type 1: autoimmune, usually children; polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, blurry vision, tiredness
Type 2: insulin resistance, genetic and lifestyle; plus recurrent infections, slow-healing sores
Glucose 4 to 7.5; hypo under 4; hyper over 7.5 fasting or 11.1 two hours after meals
Rheumatic fever: autoimmune, after an untreated strep throat; fever, aching joints, jerky movements, heart problems, up to 5 weeks later
Mostly Māori and Pacific children and teenagers; crowded housing
Penicillin injections every 28 days; rheumatic heart disease

chapters.title: The multi-choice: clinical facts
chapters.why: Forty marks are multi-choice, and the lecturers' own Canvas quizzes are the only questions of theirs that exist. These are the keys from those quizzes that no short-answer track says, clinical side first. Lisa on 27 Oct: think of the answer before you read the options.

show.ask: The lecturers' quiz keys, clinical side (1 mark each)

t: RR 32 = tachypnoea; HR 48 = bradycardia; over 100 = tachycardia
Below 35 °C = hypothermia; fever = pyrexia (39.6 °C is pyrexic)
Apnoea = no breathing; dyspnoea = short of breath
Respirations are the vital sign most under conscious control
Sphygmomanometer measures BP
EWS: recognise and respond to deterioration
Pain charted PRN 4-hourly: first assess
Donning: hand hygiene, gown, mask, goggles, gloves
Standard precautions: any time you are exposed to body fluids
Documentation: black pen; error = line, initial, "error"; no gaps so nothing can be added
Independent nursing intervention: vital signs
Short-term goal: walk 100 m unaided within a week
Care plan needs revising: frequent hypos; working: pain 2 out of 10
Fractured ribs = acute pain; immobile = risk for impaired skin integrity
NANDA before 2002: North American Nursing Diagnosis Association
Gillick competence: true
Consent: obtained by whoever does the procedure

chapters.title: The multi-choice: population and professional facts
chapters.why: The rest of the lecturers' quiz keys that no short-answer track says, from Lisa's side and the professional topics: public health, the Code of Conduct, advocacy and the Practice Quizzes captured on 27 Oct.

show.ask: The lecturers' quiz keys, population and professional side (1 mark each)

t: Whooping cough = pertussis
Smokefree: protect non-smokers, encourage quitting
Water quality: hydration, preventing waterborne disease
Key epidemiology term: incidence rate
Experimental study: actively changes a disease's progress
Equity: tailoring services to each patient's needs
Low education: limited health literacy
Code of Conduct: principle 1 dignity and individuality; principle 8 public trust and confidence
Family and patient disagree: the nurse advocates
Telemedicine helps people far from care
Long-term conditions were called chronic conditions
Hypertension plus diabetes plus asthma = multimorbidity
COPD: smoking cessation
Interdependence: the person in their wider social context
Holistic: physical, psychological, social, spiritual
Family member reports mother's pain = secondary source
Auscultating heart sounds is objective, not subjective
Hand hygiene: most effective infection control
EBP: Cochrane; clinical expertise = skills from experience

chapters.title: Rapid-fire: every answer, back to back
